name: Product catalog recall matching API
demand: Demand signals show recurring safety alerts, not the size of the paying market: the European Commission recorded 4,671 Safety Gate alerts and 5,794 follow-up actions for 2025; Safety Gate covers dangerous non-food products and excludes food, pharmaceuticals and medical devices (event year 2025: https://op.europa.eu/webpub/just/safety-gate-2025-report/en/). CPSC reported 542 recalls and safety warnings issued in 2025 (report published 2026-01-20: https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/2026/President-Trumps-CPSC-Highlights-Key-2025-Safety-Accomplishments). Amazon reported more than 75,000 independent sellers exceeded $1 million in its store in 2025; that is a buyer proxy, not a count of relevant catalog owners or willing buyers (https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/small-business/amazon-2025-small-business-empowerment-report). Total relevant buyer population, installs, users and monthly search volume are unverified; Google Keyword Planner can report average monthly searches, but no keyword figures were verified here (https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6325025?hl=en-en).
prices: The lead lists $29/month for Starter, $79/month for Growth and $199/month for Scale; these are asking prices, not proof of payment (https://recallsapi.com/pricing). Other listed offers include Recalert at $29/month for up to 500 SKUs and $99/month for up to 10,000 SKUs (https://recalert.us/en/pricing); RecallDash at $19.99/month for up to 2,000 SKUs, with Square sync or CSV where available (https://recalldash.app/pricing); and Oredrift’s EU Safety Gate API, free during early access (https://recalls.oredrift.com/). RecallDocket’s third-party app listing shows $19 and $49 plans, but also says the app is unavailable and has zero reviews, so treat it as weak evidence of a current offer (https://pickyourapp.com/products/recalldocket). RecallGuard lists $0.10 per match, but documents only an operator self-test settlement, not customer revenue (https://recallguard-docs.vercel.app/).
copy_speed: The cheap-check premise that no second dated direct launch was found is now contradicted by two dated entries since April 2026. RecallDocket’s third-party listing reports a May 19, 2026 launch for Shopify catalog matching and daily CPSC monitoring, but marks the app unavailable and shows zero reviews (https://pickyourapp.com/products/recalldocket). RecallGuard’s own docs say it was built 2026-09-28 and offers CPSC/openFDA feed and inventory matching at $0.10 per match; the docs report a 2026-09-29 operator self-test and a webhook route returning 404, so it demonstrates copy speed more than proven commercial traction (https://recallguard-docs.vercel.app/). RecallMatching also describes a catalog matching API, but its launch date is unverified and it is presented as early access (https://recallmatching.com/).
platform_risk: The core data is reproducible: CPSC offers a public machine-readable recall API to businesses and developers (https://www.cpsc.gov/Recalls/CPSC-Recalls-Application-Program-Interface-API-Information), and recallsapi.com says the government records it republishes are public domain (https://recallsapi.com/docs/data). The lead’s documented coverage is US agency data; its own source page says state and non-US recalls are out of scope, FSIS daily updates are coming soon, and some FDA feeds are not yet connected (https://recallsapi.com/docs/data). That limits its global proposition and creates feed freshness and coverage risk. Product matching is safety-sensitive: the lead itself says a match needs review and no match is not a safety certification (https://recallsapi.com/docs/). CPSC says selling recalled products is unlawful (https://www.cpsc.gov/About-CPSC/Division-of-Field-Operations/FAQs-For-Buying-and-Selling-Products-Online?language=en), so false negatives, stale feeds or overstated claims could cause serious customer harm. Shopify App Store distribution adds review and policy risk; Shopify says requirements can change and apps may be rejected (https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/launch/shopify-app-store/app-store-requirements).
defensible_asset: Potential data and switching-cost moat, currently weak. The service’s value layer is normalized identifiers, confidence explanations, source freshness, catalog monitoring and retained match/dismissal history (https://recallsapi.com/docs/monitoring; https://recallsapi.com/docs/check). But its own source documentation identifies the underlying US agency data as public domain, and customer-specific catalog history does not establish a shared proprietary correction corpus or network effect (https://recallsapi.com/docs/data). The moat becomes more credible only if it accumulates validated product-to-recall links, corrections and historical decisions with rights to retain and use them; no evidence of that cross-customer asset or material switching costs was found.
build_effort: Moderate to high, with ongoing data operations. A narrow US launch needs feed ingestion, identifier normalization, matching and confidence rules, catalog imports, alert delivery, source freshness checks and a review history; the lead documents these workflows but does not provide independent quality or reliability evidence (https://recallsapi.com/docs/monitoring; https://recallsapi.com/docs/data). Deterministic ingestion, matching, retries, billing and routine support can be automated; a person still needs to handle ambiguous safety matches, feed failures, coverage disputes and high-impact customer escalations. Adding UK and EU sources is additional jurisdiction-specific work, not a small toggle (https://recalls.oredrift.com/; https://op.europa.eu/webpub/just/safety-gate-2025-report/en/).
channel: Use inbound-only distribution: technical SEO and documentation, public API directories such as RapidAPI, and approved app marketplace listings such as Shopify; seek integrations through opt-in partner directories or inbound interest. Oredrift demonstrates a RapidAPI listing (https://rapidapi.com/oredrift-catalogue/api/eu-product-recall-safety-gate-api), and Shopify publishes app review and listing requirements (https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/launch/shopify-app-store/app-store-requirements). Paid search is another possible inbound channel if the ad and claims comply with the target jurisdiction’s rules. No cold email, SMS, DM or calls.
owner_hours_per_week: Unverified. No public operating-hours evidence establishes the ≤5 h/week limit. That cap is plausible only for a narrow, self-serve product after stable automation; feed incidents, false-positive disputes and customer onboarding could exceed it (https://recallsapi.com/docs/data; https://recallsapi.com/docs/monitoring).
automation_reason: 65% is an estimate, not a measured operating result. Scheduled source checks, normalization, matching, signed alerts, billing and routine documentation/support can run automatically or through agents (https://recallsapi.com/docs/monitoring; https://recallsapi.com/pricing). Human review remains necessary for uncertain matches and source or safety escalations because the product explicitly does not make a safety determination (https://recallsapi.com/docs/).
moat_assessment: Does not yet demonstrate the required strong moat. It has a plausible maintained-data asset and some per-customer history switching cost, but public-domain source records are easy to obtain, competitors already normalize and match them, and no network effect or proprietary shared correction corpus is evidenced (https://recallsapi.com/docs/data; https://recallsapi.com/docs/monitoring; https://recallguard-docs.vercel.app/; https://recallmatching.com/). Treat the moat as an objective to build, not an existing defensible advantage.
desk_test: One workday, without contacting anyone: use Google Keyword Planner to check buyer-intent terms in the intended launch regions; it reports average monthly search data and requires Ads account setup with billing information (https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6325025?hl=en-en). In parallel, replay a sample of product barcodes from Open Food Facts against official recall records and manually inspect candidate matches; follow its API and ODbL conditions and remember its user-submitted data is not guaranteed accurate (https://openfoodfacts.github.io/openfoodfacts-server/api/; https://www.cpsc.gov/Recalls/CPSC-Recalls-Application-Program-Interface-API-Information). This tests search demand and basic match quality, not willingness to pay; do not treat it as price validation.
red_flags: No verified customer revenue, churn, retention, subscriber count, installations or paid conversion was found. The pricing page proves listed offers and Stripe checkout availability, not completed customer payments (https://recallsapi.com/pricing). The only dated payment example from the closest newly launched API competitor is explicitly an operator self-test, not customer revenue (https://recallguard-docs.vercel.app/). The prior scarcity argument needs updating: dated direct or adjacent launches include RecallDocket and RecallGuard, while live offers include Recalert and RecallDash (https://pickyourapp.com/products/recalldocket; https://recallguard-docs.vercel.app/; https://recalert.us/en/pricing; https://recalldash.app/pricing). Search demand, acquisition cost, false-negative rate, actual support load and the ≤5 h/week constraint remain unverified.
